query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic behavior of solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature‐ and strain-rate–dependent transition between dislocation glide and deformation twinning, mediated by variations in stacking fault energy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy with an equiatomic, homogeneous microstructure and minimal pre-existing defects.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to mechanical loading tests over a range of temperatures (cryogenic, room temperature, and elevated) and strain rates (from quasi-static to high rate dynamic loading).
generation.conditions: Controlled laboratory environment with precisely maintained temperatures and strain rates. Samples must be as-solidified without additional thermomechanical treatments to preserve the baseline microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Stacking fault energy, which modulates the relative ease of activating dislocation glide versus deformation twinning.
generation.mechanism: At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, higher effective stacking fault energy favors dislocation glide, yielding ductile mechanical response. In contrast, at lower temperatures and/or higher strain rates, a reduction in stacking fault energy promotes deformation twinning, thereby increasing work hardening and altering the dynamic response.
generation.predicted_outcome: A distinct transition in the deformation mechanism is expected: under cryogenic/high strain-rate conditions, increased twin formation alongside enhanced work hardening, while under high temperature/quasi-static conditions, the deformation is predominantly mediated by dislocation glide with lower twin density.
generation.baseline: Mechanical response and microstructural evolution characterized at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to as-solidified, minimally processed FeNiCrMn alloys; in alloys with significant prior work (e.g., cold work or aging) or in radically different composition ranges, the mechanism may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contribution of the two deformation modes and the exact stacking fault energy values across the temperature/strain-rate conditions remain to be determined and may exhibit complexities beyond a simple transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare as-solidified FeNiCrMn samples and perform a series of mechanical tests at selected temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room, and elevated temperatures) and across a range of strain rates (from quasi-static to high rate). Employ in situ microscopic techniques such as TEM or EBSD during loading to directly observe the presence and evolution of dislocation structures and twinning.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to capture work hardening trends under different loading conditions.
In situ imaging (TEM/EBSD) to detect the onset and density of deformation twins versus dislocation patterns.
XRD to monitor any phase changes or additional defect formations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if, across the range of temperature and strain-rate conditions, there is no observable shift from dislocation glide to deformation twinning (i.e., no significant increase in twin density at low temperatures/high strain rates) or if the mechanical responses (e.g., work hardening rates) do not correlate with the predicted shift in deformation mechanism.
